title: Mary Yearwood vs Caribbean Investments Ltd (Casuarina Property)

FINDING OF TRIBUNAL ON QUESTION(S) OF FACT MATERIAL TO DECISION 

The Tribunal finds that: 

(i) 

(ii) 

(iii) 

(iv) 

(v) 

The Respondent dismissed the Claimant on April 9, 2015; 

Having been employed on December 7, 2009, at the time of dismissal the 
Claimant had been employed in excess of one (1) year ( five (5) complete 
years); 

The principal reason for the Claimants’ dismissal was redundancy. 

Dismissal of the Claimant represented a reduction of 25% of the 
Respondent’s workforce; 

The Respondent did not carry out consultations with the Claimant prior to 
her dismissal; and 

(vi) 

The Claimants were unfairly dismissed. 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

SUMMARY OF DECISION 

Introduction 

The Claimant began working with the Respondent as a cook on or about December 7, 2009. The 
Respondent alleges that the reason for the Claimant’s dismissal was due to a reorganisation that resulted 
in it no longer having a requirement for a full time cook. In these circumstances the Respondent contends 
that it terminated the Claimant’s employment with the Respondent on or about April 9, 2015 due to 
redundancy. 

Finding of Facts 

The Tribunal finds that: 

1. 

2. 

At the time of their dismissal the Claimants were employed for over a year. It is a 
finding of fact that having been employed from December 7, 2009 to April 9, 2015 the 
Claimant was employed for a period of five (5) complete years. 

Therefore the Claimant has acquired the right not to be unfairly dismissed by the 
Respondent pursuant to Section 27 of the Employment Rights Act, 2012-9 (the 
“Act”). 

3. 

The Claimant in her evidence in chief given by way of witness statement stated that: 

Matters began to change drastically when Bajan Services Limited took over; 
whereas I had the responsibility to draw up food lists. These were now being 
handled by the House Manager without consulting me. 

4. 

5. 

6. 

7. 

This evidence is buttressed by the Respondent’s evidence in chief given by Gina-Lee 
Johnson by way of witness Statement (the “Johnson Statement”) where she stated at 
paragraph 8 it was decided that the Respondent would restructure the staffing at 
Casuarina to include a temporary Sous-Chef only when the property was occupied. 

The evidence above is suggests that the requirements of the Respondent for a cook to 
carry out work of a particular kind at the Casuarina Property had diminished. This is 
consistent with the definition of redundancy outlined in the Act1. 

The Tribunal is of the view that the Claimant was in fact dismissed as a result of 
redundancy. 

Having found that the Claimant was dismissed as a result of redundancy, the Tribunal 
must determine whether the dismissal complied with the requirements of the Act. 

Was the Claimant's dismissal compliant with the Act? 

8. 

9. 

10. 

According to paragraph 4 of the Johnson Statement, at the time that Bajan Services 
Limited took over the management of the Casuarina Property there was a staff 
compliment of four (4) people; the Claimant – cook, Beulah Worrell – Housekeeper, 
Bernard Francis – Gardener and Judy Sober – Assistant Gardener. 

To the extent that dismissal of the Claimant due to redundancy represented a reduction 
of 25% of the Respondent’s workforce; the Act required the Respondent to engage in 
consultations with the Claimant not less than 6 weeks before the Claimant (or indeed 
any other employee who could be made redundant) was dismissed for redundancy2. 

There is no evidence that the Respondent conducted the required consultations. 
Instead as stated at paragraph 8 of the Johnson Statement, the Respondent purported 
to pay the Claimant 6 weeks in lieu of Consultation. The Tribunal is unaware of any 
legal authority that supports the action taken by the Respondent. 

11. 

In the circumstances, the Tribunal is of the view that the dismissal of the Claimant 
contravened the right conferred on her by Section 27 of the Act3. 

1 Employment Rights Act; Section 31 (2) (b). 
2 Employment Rights Act; Section 31 (6) (a). 
3 Employment Rights Act; Section 31 (1). 

 
 
 

12. 

The Claimant was therefore unfairly dismissed. 

What is the appropriate remedy? 

13. 

14. 

Having determined that the Claimant was unfairly dismissed the Tribunal takes note of 
the Claimant’s claim for relief as set out in her “Computation of Relief Claimed by Mary 
Yearwood”. 

The Tribunal accepts that the Claimant is not interested in reinstatement or re-
engagement but was instead interested in financial compensation. 

Basic Award 

15. 

16. 

The Claimant is entitled to receive a basic award pursuant to Section 1 (a) of the Fifth 
Schedule of the Act. 

The Respondent employed the Claimant for a period of five (5) complete years. At 
paragraph 7 of the Claimant’s witness statement, she stated that her gross earnings 
for the income year 2014 were $22,598.58. Using this figure, her week’s basic would 
be $434.58 (22,598,58 ÷ 52). Pursuant to the formula set out at Section 2 (2) of the 
Fifth Schedule of the Act, the Claimant is entitled to a basic award in the sum of 
$5,432.25. This sum being her weekly wage of $434.58 multiplied by 2.5 multiplied by 
5 being the number of years she was employed. 

Further Awards 

17. 

As indicated by the Caribbean Court of Justice: 

…the basic award serves a dual purpose of both retrospective compensation 
for years of service rendered as well as prospective compensation for loss of 
wages following a dismissal. As such, there was no room for the ERA to 
provide for a separate award for loss of wages. In claiming for expected 
benefits, it would be for an employee to provide evidence of such benefits, and 
for the ERT to award such amount as it thinks fit.4 

18. 

19. 

Consequentially, the Claimants claim for $20,354.64 (a year’s wages) must be 
rejected. 

Though the Tribunal may have been minded to consider a claim for lost tips; said tips 
being a benefit, there is not sufficient evidence before the Tribunal to award the sum 
of $3,640.00 as claimed. The Claimant’s evidence at paragraph 7 of her witness 
statement was that “Any tips I received were minimal in any event.” This statement 
cannot be reconciled with what amounts to $303.33 per month in tips. For this reason, 
the Tribunal must also reject the Claimant’s claim for a “discretionary award”. 

20. 

Section 2 (5) of the Fifth Schedule of the Act states that: 

The amount determined in accordance with the rules set out in subparagraphs 
(2) to (4) shall be reduced by the amount of 

(a) 

(b) 

any severance payment paid by the employer to the employee 
under the Severance Payments Act in respect of the same 
dismissal; or 
any payment made by the employer to the employee, whether 
in pursuance of the Severance Payments Act or otherwise, on 
the ground that the dismissal was by reason of redundancy. 

21. 

During her oral evidence 5 the Claimant indicated that she received the sum of 
$5,490.75 as a severance payment. This sum is consistent with the sum reflected at 
being “purportedly paid as severance” in her “Computation of Relief Claimed by Mary 
Yearwood”. This sum must therefore be deducted from any basic award granted to the 

4 Judgment Summary CCJ Appeal No. BBCV2019/0037 Chefette Restaurants Limited v Orlando Harris at paragraph 
16. 
5 November 11, 2022 

 
 

Respondent. This exercise would result in a negative balance ($5,432.25 - $5,490.75 
= -$58.50). 

22. 

For this reason the Tribunal makes no further award to the Claimant in respect of her 
unfair dismissal. 

REASON FOR DISSENT (IF ANY) 

N/A
